reviews.text: I want to get into the mind of Alfred Hitchcock because the premise of this movie is so unique that I did not fully understand the ending until 2 hours after watching. James Stewart is an actor in his own league; his name defines this generation of acting that cannot be replicated. His acting is impeccable in this film, and the insanity of his character is something that will stay with me long after I've forgotten the plot of the movie itself.
It was alright, the twists were good and unexpected but the movie was weird and I couldn’t get into it most of the time. It’s good but not as good as people say.

oh come on now, the painting wasn't that bad... e imagina tener que perseguir a tu novia para que no se MATE. La obsesión de Hitchcock por tirar a gente de ventanas??? A ver. La peli es una pasada, ya solo por los planos, los colores, por Kim Novak, el vestuario, el diseño de interiores... todo eso me encantó. No era la primera vez que la veía, pero no recordaba casi nada. Sencillamente creo, que tenía muchas expectativas. Me gustó más estéticamente que la historia en sí. No me enganchó tanto como otras, pese a que los actores son increíbles y la química es muy buena. Ha sido un día bastante triste para mí, así que sé que si la vuelvo a ver me gustará más. Seguiremos viendo.

I did not feel like I was ever on the same page with this film LMFAO. Like I do respect the big swings being taken. There are some genuinely stunning visuals and lots of pieces of the story I find compelling and interesting, but somehow they just don’t quite slot together for me…? But maybe that’s the point?????? I DONT KNOWWWW I DONT KNOW !!!!!!!!!! also the people behind me in the theater were eating popcorn louder than i’ve ever heard someone eat popcorn before so maybe that hurt the experience some. anyway ummmmmmmm mmmmmmmmmmmmmmmm maybe i’ll wake up tomorrow and understand everything idk. glad to finally get this off my watchlist at least

First Alfred Hitchcock movie. I really liked the old, dated style of the movie and the simple camera techniques used that you don’t see in modern movies. Love San Francisco asthetic in the 50’s. However this film wasn’t all that it was hyped up to be from the reviews and ratings I’ve seen. Some of the scenes are a little unbelievable how they are happening and honestly kinda just make you laugh especially the ending that was pretty bad wasn’t a fan. Upon further research and understanding what the film stands for and it’s trying to convey it made it more interesting to reflect on but I think it could have been done better with the twist being done in a less cliche way. Still a solid movie and enjoyable watch but not the best film of all time the way some people see it.

This movie is great in its climatic parts, especially in the last act of the movie. I just wish it was not super slow at some parts, especially in the middle where it sets up the importance. It just slowed down the narrative and that momentum so much.

vertigo é realmente um filme incrível. mas minha expectativa estava muito alta e, talvez por isso a nota tenha ficado “baixa”. talvez ela mude com o tempo, porque com certeza vou assistir mais vezes. a direção segue o nível do hitchcock, e a movimentação da câmera é muito boa. as cores são bem marcantes, elas fazem o filme parecer uma pintura. as atuações também são ótimas, james stewart talvez seja meu ator “antigo” favorito. algumas coisas não envelhecem muito bem, mas isso é normal, considerando o ano de lançamento. mas a parte que mais me incomodou foi o romance do filme. ele parece surgir do nada e, na minha opinião é arrastado desde o início. acho que mais admirei do que gostei de assistir. tecnicamente é absurdo e tem várias cenas marcantes, e pode ser um daqueles filmes que crescem depois de reassistir.

Very good movie and the amazing use of color was stunning. The last 40 minutes of the movie were spectacular. I can absolutely see why this is called one of the greatest movies ever made but if we talk about best... it's just not (for me). Maybe it needs a rewatch.

Una muy buena historia de misterio que enlaza lo paranormal con la acrofobia. Los colores elegidos son fantásticos, tiene planos altamente memorables y giros de guión bastante sorprendentes para la época.

What a movie! For it being a psychological thriller, i think the giveaway of the plot twist happens way too soon. The only flaw for me is that we as viewers should have found out the twist along with Scottie. Other than that the movie is quite devastating. It’s about fear, obsession and how love can be and how it can take you to some really twisted places. I think it also shows how men can have this obsession with wanting something untouchable and fantasy-like, something they can’t have. The women other than Madeleine, Midge and Judy are both great women with good personalities who genuinely care for Scottie. Yet he seems to crave something that doesn’t make sense. His obsession with Madeleine is something you can’t really put a finger on. It also kind of shows how women are treated as desirable objects in the film and how they are desired only if they are a certain way. Anyway, lastly, the movie had very little to do with what “vertigo” actually is lol but regardless of that, it is a great movie!

It's unusual for me to choose an old movie to watch, but this one has been mentioned enough times in comments and such that I decided to see it and get acquainted with the classics. I knew nothing about the movie. Several times just past the mid point of the movie before the reveal, I expected it to end abruptly without any explanation. I was so happy to see the amount of time left. The reveal/flashback made all the difference for me. It got interesting after that. My mom guessed the culprits within the first twenty minutes. I was only hoping that there wouldn't be anything supernatural. I really should watch more Hitchcock movies. I think I'm ready to handle them! It will be difficult for me to not ask questions though. I really enjoyed seeing San Francisco! It's hard to believe that this was filmed almost seventy years ago! I kept waiting for Midge. The alternative ending gave me comfort. I agree that the lead actor was too old for his part. But the man had to be old in order to retire! I didn't notice a single non-white actor in the whole movie. I doubt that San Francisco was like that in the 50s. But in general, there are very few people shown in the streets.

Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo reminds us that a movie, no matter the age, with a compelling story, engaging characters, and a genius use of visual techniques can create an entertaining cinematic experience. This movie shines in all these categories and, personally, has made this film a personal favorite of mine.  The first aspect of the film I really enjoyed was the emphasis on color as meaning. Hitchcock was a master at showing and not telling with a film, and this movie really proves that. The film’s Technicolor made Hitchcock’s storytelling through color really shine. You can tell when the film intends to invoke a certain idea or emotion, such as Madeleine’s silhouette shots with the green neon lights from the hotel sign illuminating the space. It seemed as though green invoked a sense of mystery to Madeleine’s character as Scottie slowly began to unravel the truth behind her aura. The color red also comes into play as it helps emphasize Scottie’s slow turn to obsession and lust for Madeleine’s image. The ultra-vibrant Red restaurant, a strong example of this technique, started to appear more frequently as Scottie began to spiral into psychological obsession. Another technique I really appreciated was the film’s pacing. Vertigo highlighted the importance of setting the plot with a slow start, and using that slow pace to parallel a sense of mystery and suspense. This film didn’t feed action in every scene; it kept the audience intrigued by creating a compelling case. The compelling Madeline case made me pay attention to the film even more, and as I realized, it surely rewarded me in the end with the movie’s signature twist. Pacing is really important because the more you pay attention, the more the film rewards you. To be honest, Vertigo did not challenge me in any of its aspects. Honestly, it was really refreshing watching a film that was slow and long because it helped me feel more connected to the story. This film did not feel forced or rushed; the unique story felt authentic to human experience. The psychological aspect of the film felt real because obsession, no matter what it can be about, could be experienced by anyone. With the success of the movie Obsession in 2026, I can see some similarities between both. Now, this doesn’t mean Vertigo Is the 1950s version of Obsession, but I can see some parallels between Bear’s character and Scottie's character. Both characters form a perfect image of their women, and with this obsession, slowly evolve from innocent loveable characters, to serious toxic individuals. After watching Obsession, I do have a better understanding of Vertigo. Watching Obsession helped me understand Scottie’s character on a much deeper level, especially because of the parallels with Bear. I could somehow know what Scottie was feeling and how his obsession would cause harm to his life after recalling what Bear went through in Obsession. In conclusion, Alfred Hitchcock’s Vertigo deserves to be recognized as a true classic. Its compelling, suspenseful, and rewarding story stands out among many modern films.
Movie was so interesting and also just great to look at. But there are parts of the story I just cant shake my head into agreeing with. Watched by myself and a bit with my beautiful girl

I really enjoyed this movie because it was really interesting and mysterious. It really kept me thinking what would happen next and if Madeleine would ever notice him spying on her. When Madeleine died it really made me uneasy because Scottie become a new person and he really acted strangely, he forced Judy into becoming Madeleine which was just weird and I did not like that part of the movie. The colors were really vibrant in the movie, and it made me think what they could mean. When Scottie was in the restaurant seeing Madeleine for the first time the wall and floor was red which probably signified danger because ever since he started following her, his life just started going downhill. Her dress was green which represents mysteriousness which signifies that Madeleine is a mysterious person in the beginning of the movie because we knew nothing about her just that she goes into a trance from time to time. When Scottie had that dream and his face became green, I think they used that color to signify mysteriousness because he has never experienced that before until the death of “Madeleine.” All the colors in that sequence were just very unsettling because they were flashing and maybe meant danger or that he might lose his mind. The Camera shots were really good especially all the cinematic ones. One scene that really stood out to me was when they were at the church after Madeleine jumped off and Scottie was in the bottom right leaving the scene while the saints were climbing onto the roof and checking the body of Madeleine. I think this Scene really showed us the sense of fear that Scottie felt that he couldn’t stay there and talked to the saints who were checking. The Shots of the redwood forest really captivated me because it looked so beautiful and really wants me to go there and see them myself. Personally, I thought the beginning of the movie was really slow and kind of boring but ever since he talked to Gavin and made the plan to follow his wife that was when it really ramped up and it very interesting. It kind of made me reconsider my cardinal sin because I should be patient with movies because typically the beginning is always boring and slow but as it goes on it starts to get better. In conclusion for a movie that came out like 70 years ago it was really interesting and mysterious. I would definitely recommend this movie to some of my friends that aren’t in Film Arts and to my family.

what if you loved someone so much you stopped letting them be gone? he wasn't in love with her, he was in love with the version of her he couldn't let go of. watching scottie rebuild someone from memory feels less like romance and more like watching grief become an obsession.

On 16mm film at the Art Theatre Long Beach (16mm!!!! Tiny!) A masterpiece of filmmaking - the camera angles, the acting, the writing, the colours (my god the colours). The plot keeps you guessing all the way through, and that descent into madness from Jimmy Stewart after Madeline's death is absolutely impeccable. He's obsessed & traumatized like nothing else. A note for 16mm film - it was beautiful and lovely but man some of the physical print had not aged well - sections were dark, it was not very crisp, parts were damaged and some sections of sound were quite distracting. Not to say it wasn't worth it, because it was, but man I'd love to have watched this on 35mm or 70mm, if only for the colours that make Vertigo so famous.

My Vertigo watching experience was magical but also intense at the same time.  The scene where Scottie was spying on Madeleine at the flower shop was a scene with breathtaking colors that caught my eye. I began to pay attention to the colors throughout the movie and I began to appreciate how much work the editors must've put. The colors especially at the flower shop created the illusion of a dream-like atmosphere and I couldn't help but to admire. During the confrontation between Scottie and Judy at the church, the camera was zoomed super close to both Judy's and Scottie's faces heightening the tension between the two. While watching the confrontation, I became super invested and I had forgotten about the slow-pacing of the first half of the movie. It was as if I was watching them argue in real time and the shadows and the music increased the intensity of that scene. All the comedic, intense, and romantic scenes were perfectly executed to the point where I wasn't mad that the movie was moving at a slower pace compared to modern movies. At first the slow-pacing was a drawback from my watching experience but all the camera angles, colors, and music compensated for a while. This was until we reached to the second half of the movie where Scottie saved Madeleine from drowning which where the movie got interesting. Everyone behind the scenes did a great job on this movie and in my opinion, Vertigo is a classic and this movie made me reconsider watching movies on my watch list that move at a slower pace.

So that’s pretty fun! :)

Today was my 30th birthday! I took my parents out to lunch and then brought them back to my place. We were going to head out to an IMAX re-release of The Shining, but my mother didn't like the trailer, which is just the scene where a river of blood sloshes out of the elevator. My father was also unenthusiastic about my pitch for the film - "It's about the white man's murder of the Native Americans!". I also had some mild reservations about rewatching a movie I'd just watched 6 months prior. The whole point of this hobby is to broaden my horizons after all. So we decided to stay in and watch a film on my new 65" TV. I presented two alternatives - Vertigo and Goldfinger. The moment I mentioned Alfred Hitchcock and the San Francisco setting (we're in the Bay Area), my mother was sold on Vertigo. I was also excited to watch what I've regularly seen ranked as the best film ever made (alongside Citizen Kane). By coincidence, I'd just seen Vertigo star James Stewart in a holiday screening of It's a Wonderful Life, and here I got to see him go from the charismatic leader he was there to a broken, twisted man driven mad by a combination of his vertigo (phobia of heights) and trauma over his apparent love interest (the wife of a man who hired him as a private eye) committing suicide in front of him. When he finds a woman a year later who looks exactly like his lover, the mystery around his lover's suicide starts to unravel and the viewer gets disoriented so badly from the revelation that we truly understand the sensation of "vertigo" ourselves. My mother was excitedly pointing out various landmarks she recognized ("That's the presidio! That's Sausalito!") as the film progressed, and we resolved to visit more of the Bay Area together. To my and my father's amazement, she also predicted various plot points before they transpired ("She's not dead! It's a dummy!", "The necklace! He'll know it's her from the necklace!"). Philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer observed that a man inherits his intellect from his mother, and I see the truth of that. After we finished watching the movie and my parents left, I re-read Roger Ebert's essay describing the film in his Great Movies and finally had the context to appreciate it. I close with a quote from it. "As Scottie embraces “Madeleine,” even the background changes to reflect his subjective memories instead of the real room he’s in. Bernard Herrmann’s score creates a haunting, unsettled yearning. And the camera circles them hopelessly, like the pinwheel images in Scottie’s nightmares, until the shot is about the dizzying futility of our human desires, the impossibility of forcing life to make us happy. This shot, in its psychological, artistic, and technical complexity, may be the one time in his entire career that Alfred Hitchcock completely revealed himself, in all of his passion and sadness. (Is it a coincidence that the woman is named Madeleine—the word for the French biscuit which, in Proust, brings childhood memories of loss and longing flooding back?) Alfred Hitchcock took universal emotions, like fear, guilt, and lust, placed them in ordinary characters, and developed them in images more than in words. His most frequent character, an innocent man wrongly accused, inspired much deeper identification than the superficial superman in today’s action movies."

Every shot looks like a painting and the story doesn’t let you go even for a second I was actually at the edge of my seat connecting all the dots and seeing everything unfold I had an actual HOLY FUCK moment towards the end so so so incredible. Scottie’s unraveling throughout the film was incredible to watch and it was thrilling to watch his relationship with Judy evolve with the whole scheme and her guilt!! The ONLY thing I didn’t really like was Midge’s character development, just my take but I felt kind of let down in the direction where they took her character, her and John had so much chemistry at the start with their dialogues and their chill and friendly dynamic was very refreshing before she was absorbed in her infatuation with John and her devolving into this weird mother dynamic felt a little random when her arc just finished there, wish she could’ve at least contributed a little more to the narrative towards the end. Can you tell Midge was my favorite character I was going to talk about the actual film but I got too caught up rambling about her my bad….

Hitchcock's films just get better throughout the runtime, engaging for the entire plot, evolving masterfully at every point and constantly keeping the viewer on their toes whilst also being a very beautiful visual experience despite being nearly 70 years old.

Sur le podium des plus grand films de l'histoire ! Vertigo est une des tragédie les plus marquante du cinéma. Un cinéma d'époque à son apogée, une technique folle, une musique exceptionnelle. Une histoire riche, pleine de rebondissement ou le spectateur est manipulé de A à Z par le génie de Hitchcock. Il nous immerge dans la tête et les sensations de Scottie, on croit tout ce que l'on voit comme lui, mais... avant lui, on fini par comprendre, et on voit ce héros perdre la tête et céder à son obsession. Une position glaciale ou cette homme détruit une personne réel pour retrouver une illusion, pour finir sur une fin avec une "chute" horrible autant psychologiquement que physiquement... A voir absolument ! Je dirai même que si il y avait un seul film à voir, ce serait celui-ci !

Que história perfeita, meu tipo de filme preferido, um que você pensa que está entendendo a história, e o plot consegue mudar absolutamente tudo. Suspense, drama, e sempre com uma pergunta na cabeça. Ela realmente está possuída? Sinto que será difícil encontrar um plot bom assim de novo..

É, realmente, tudo depois de Vertigo é Vertigo. Que filme bonito, pode pausar em qualquer frame que dá pra usar de papel de parede. Camada por camada, ele constrói uma trama sobre obsessão que você não entende pra onde vai até que chega. É provavelmente a obra-prima absoluta do Hitchcock: seu mistério assinatura, os ângulos e a iluminação. É diferente de tudo. Filmaço impecável e o que a Kim Novak é uma INSANIDADE.

Maestro Hitchcock lo hizo otra vez, nos deleita con este drama detectivesco que poco a poco pasa a ser una historia cada vez más triste, oscura y al final trágica. Me encanta el final, aunque comprendo que sea un debate, yo creo que estuvo increíble. La película dura bastante pero creo que en ningún momento se vuelve monótona, cada escena sumamente necesaria y cinematográficamente muy bonita para lo reciente del tecnicolor.

Vertigo ▪︎ตำรวจเก่าที่กลัวความสูงได้รับการขอความช่วยเหลือจากคนรู้จักเพื่อตามสืบเมียของเขาว่าทำไมถึงชอบทำพฤติกรรมแปลก ๆ ราวกับมีวิญญาณจากใครสักคนในอดีตมาสิงร่างเธอ ▪︎ตอนจบเหวอแดกจริง ๆ คือหนังมันก็หักมุมแล้วหักมุมอีก หักจนถึงตอนจบอะ แล้วจบแบบ อ้าวเห้ย แล้วก็มีเสียงลมวิ้งๆพัดผ่านหูไป ▪︎กลางเรื่องคือมันจะแอบอึดอัด ทำไมตัวละครทำอะไรแปลก ๆ งงงวย ไม่สมเหตุสมผล แต่พอเจอเหตุการณ์ใหญ่บนหอคอยไปก็อึ้งกิมกี่ ก่อนค่อย ๆ เฉลยต่อมา *สปอยล์* ▪︎หยิบเอาเรื่องกลัวความสูงมาเล่น การทำแผนการตบตาที่ชาญฉลาดแต่แกมโกงของผู้ว่าจ้าง ที่เอาความไม่ปกติของตัวเอกมาทำให้พล็อตการฆาตกรรมอำพรางมันซับซ้อน และแทบจะไม่สามารถแก้ไขได้เลย ถ้าสุดท้ายเรื่องนี้ไม่มีสมการของความรักของคนที่ทำหน้าที่หลอก กับคนที่โดนหลอก ▪︎ตอนแรกก็รำคาญตัวเอกตอนเจอคนที่หลอกมากว่า ทำไมจะต้องมีนิสัยเจ้ากี้เจ้าการขนาดนั้น แต่ก็เข้าใจว่า ฮิตช์ค็อกอยากให้ความเจ้าบงการและความอาลัยกับรักเก่าเป็นตัวชี้นำไคลแมกซ์ของเรื่อง เพราะมันทำให้ใจคนดูและตัวเอกแตกสลายไปพร้อมกันว่า จบไม่สวยแน่นอน

RIP Scottie Ferguson; you would have loved the One Wish Willow. -------- For the longest time when I was younger, Vertigo was my favorite film. While it's no longer my number one, it's still a film I love a lot. So much has already been said about this film, one of the most dissected in history, so I won't get into everything that makes it so great (the score, the shots, the color, the themes, etc). But something that struck me this time, after not having seen it for a while and seeing it on the big screen, was the intensity of emotion. Not just from Scottie, a man obviously obsessed, but also Judy, a woman willing to change her whole self for the man she loves.

AFI Silver. Hitchcock/Hermann. 70mm. Everyone loves a Hitchcock film, but a Hitchcock/Hermann film? Amazing. AFI did a series of all eight films that featured the historic collaboration between director Alfred Hitchcock and musician Bernard Herrmann. Per AFI: "Hitchcock and Hermann collaborated on eight films over an 11-year period. Despite their differing backgrounds and opposite temperaments, "Benny and Hitch" formed a close working relationship, resulting in some of their most beloved and enduring works." I was able to see seven out of the eight films at AFI Silver! This was the third film I saw at AFI. This is one of my favorite films of all time, full stop. It's hard to describe just how brilliant this film is in every way, and that includes the score. As AFI states, this is "Alfred Hitchcock's supreme achievement, the fullest expression of his cinematic obsessions and the one that goes the furthest in pursuit of them." It's hard to overstate how good this film is. And seeing it on 70mm was of course a real treat.
